note: Ratchet for `scripts/loc-metrics.py`. Every number below is lines of git-tracked source, classified by the lexer in `scripts/lib/loc_classify.py`. They may only go DOWN — raising a limit to make a build green defeats the point of measuring, so a rise fails the gate. When a rise is deliberate, run `scripts/loc-metrics.py --baseline` and commit the new file in the SAME commit that grew the tree. Generated files (`@generated` / `DO NOT EDIT` in the header) are measured but excluded from these limits, because appending a wire kind must never fail a size gate. The `*.comment` numbers are measured and diffed but NOT gated: a gate that makes deleting documentation the cheapest way to go green is pointed at the wrong thing. What these limits do NOT cover, stated so the total has a denominator: the programme's own tooling, 11 `.py` files (3,434 code lines) and 25 `.sh` files (3,821), 7,255 code lines in all -- roughly 4.4% of the tree, and rising, because this tooling is inside its own blind spot. Counting them needs a `#`-comment lexer for two more languages, here-documents and docstrings included, and until that exists moving logic into a script still reads as reduction.
measured:
2026-08-10 at 51b92f5 + issue #167 (MC-JOIN-2), by `scripts/loc-metrics.py --baseline` on this branch with every file of the change already tracked. Re-measure on the merged tree before trusting it: a ratchet file describes exactly one tree and no branch's tree survives a merge.

Deliberate growth, +120 java.main.code and +214 java.test.code. Splitting the joiner's peer bring-up off the client render thread is a lifecycle split, not a move: the synchronous prologue and the off-thread body are separate methods, the body needs a discard path for everything it built but never published, and cancellation needs a generation counter and an in-flight flag because `clientRuntime != null` stops being a re-entrancy guard the moment the runtime is built off-thread. The announce moved with it, from the payload handler into its own method on the bring-up thread. The test growth is two new files, `ClientBringUpIsOffTheRenderThreadTest` and `NoderaPeerServiceBringUpCancellationTest`, plus the `ContinuityScenario` stage that bounds the client thread live.

The first stamp of this change read +16 java.test.code, because `--baseline` measures `git ls-files` and the two new test files were not yet added when it ran. The order is always `git add` -> `--baseline` -> `--check`; CI caught it as `java.test.code: 55147 -> 55345`, which is why this file has a second commit on it.

The previous stamp's note -- which explains the PR #222 reduction wave, the Kotlin bucket entering the gate, and the Rust `#[cfg(test)] mod` lexer correction -- is in git history on this file; it described a tree this one is downstream of.

Every bucket sits exactly on its measured value, because that is what `--baseline` writes; there is never any headroom, so a one-line fix and its test cost a stamp. That pressure is the known cost of an exact ratchet, and the answer to it is a reason recorded here, not a limit with slack in it.
